questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn WITHOUT replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: P(1st red) = 5/8. P(2nd red | 1st red) = 4/7. P(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. Options (b) and (d) are the same value. Option (a) incorrectly uses 5/8 × 5/8, treating it as with replacement.

questions.stem: A jar has 6 green and 4 yellow sweets. Two sweets are taken without replacement. What is the probability of getting one of each colour?
questions.explanation: P(green then yellow) = 6/10 × 4/9 = 24/90. P(yellow then green) = 4/10 × 6/9 = 24/90. P(one of each) = 24/90 + 24/90 = 48/90 = 8/15. A common error is only considering one order.

questions.stem: A box has 3 defective and 7 working light bulbs. Two bulbs are selected without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is defective?
questions.explanation: P(at least 1 defective) = 1 − P(both working) = 1 − (7/10 × 6/9) = 1 − 42/90 = 1 − 7/15 = 8/15. Using the complement method is much easier than adding all favourable cases.

questions.stem: A bag contains 8 balls: 2 red, 3 blue, 3 green. Two balls are picked without replacement. What is the probability of picking two blue balls?
questions.explanation: P(1st blue) = 3/8. P(2nd blue | 1st blue) = 2/7. P(both blue) = 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. Options (b) and (c) are the same value in different forms.

questions.stem: There are 12 chocolates in a box: 5 milk and 7 dark. Three are eaten without replacement. What is the probability all three are dark?
questions.explanation: P = 7/12 × 6/11 × 5/10 = 210/1320 = 7/44. Each draw reduces both the number of dark chocolates and the total. Option (a) uses 7/12 three times (with replacement error).
